chapter: Growing up with jazz in Belfast
title: First jazz records and the school band in Belfast
summary: Pee Wee Hunt, Bunk Johnson and Condon records, a school band on which he played trombone, and Ken Smiley's Belfast band.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Well, the first record I ever heard that I could even class as jazz was Pee Wee Hunt's record, The 12th Street Rag, which came out when I was about 14. And that was the first time I ever noticed jazz, you know. And then I was in school in Ireland, in Belfast, in boarding school, and all we had to do was listen to records. And some fellows got interested in jazz. There's a band in Belfast. They're always, they were a Dixieland band, and they always got very offended when anybody ever mentioned the Dixieland revival, because they played straight through. They kind of copied the Muggsy records of the late 30s, and they never stopped through the entire war, right through to when I got interested, you see. And they played for our high school dances, so forth. Ken Smiley's band, he's since given up music and went into the newspaper business, and he was the guy that handled Louis' tour to West Africa. He's high up now in the newspaper business. He's quit playing the trumpet. He's a Belfast man. And they played, and the fellows who bought the records that I first listened to, this sounds like total recall, but I guess it's what you want. Whatever. Yeah. They used to listen to him. And they bought a lot of Chicago stuff, pretty indiscriminate taste in buying the music. You know, you'd get all kinds of bad stuff. But they bought all the Bunk records which were available in England at that time, all of them on HMV, and none of them available in this country at the present time, to my knowledge, or ever have been, recorded late after about 47, I think. 47. 46 maybe. I don't, I think more than 47. And all sorts of other stuff. Wingy Manone, that kind of thing, you know. Chicago stuff. Condon, they all bought the Condon records. And Bunny Berrigan playing I Can't Get Started. That's one of the first records I ever, you know. I would still like it as much as I did then. Sure. That kind of thing.

And I remember the fellow, the fellow, we had a little band in school, you know, and I played trombone on it at that time. I used to play trombone. And he, he liked to imitate Bobby Hackett, that kind of stuff, you know, sort of late Chicago smooth stuff. And we played the odd job, again, at high school dances. And I remember he played me a Bunk Johnson record once and I asked him about the clarinet player, Lewis, and he said, oh yes, Lewis. Never heard the name. I was very impressed that he knew the name of somebody else who wasn't listed on the label. He said, yes, very old style that. He said, it's not much good. Nothing to compare with Pee Wee or somebody like that, which sounds funny now. When you consider the amount of fuss made about Lewis and how Pee Wee's kind of fallen, fallen off. And I play, we had this little band, I played trombone with them. And then, and I, we, and the first band I ever heard was that Ken Smiley band, which is a pretty smooth band. I think it would have held up, it would have held up pretty well by any standards, you know. It was, it was good white Dixieland.
They just got sort of tired of playing or something?

No, they, no, they, it went on and on. The big, the good, the better fellas in the band dropped out because they got better jobs and left Belfast. Yeah. But you see, they were stuck in Belfast through the entire war years. There was a kind of a little jazz continuity going on in Belfast because there wasn't any war in Northern Ireland to speak of. There was no conscription, for instance. Yeah. You see. And there, but of course, if they'd gone to England to get better jobs, as they could have got, then they would have been drafted. So they stuck on there and played. And then when the war got over and they got too old to get drafted, then they went and got good jobs in England and were, well, like Smiley, I was saying, was posted to West Africa working for the Daily Mirror.
